questions.question: Which of the following provides the most detailed three-dimensional view of the structure of the living human brain? i. PET ii . angiography iii. EEG iv. MRI
questions.solution_html:
• Answer: iv. MRI
  • Cerebral Cortex: The convoluted outer layer of the brain.
  • Thalamus
  • o Structure: A paired, egg-shaped structure.
  • o Function: The "Gateway to the Cortex." It processes and relays almost all
  • sensory information (except smell) to the appropriate primary sensory areas of
  • the cerebral cortex. It also plays a role in regulating consciousness, sleep, and
  • alertness.
  • Sexually Dimorphic Nucleus of the Preoptic Area (SDN-POA)
  • Location: Preoptic Area of the hypothalamus.
  • Difference: This nucleus is significantly larger (2-3 times) and contains more
  • neurons in males than in females across many species, including humans (where it is
  • called the INAH-3).
  • Functional Significance: The SDN-POA is crucial for the expression of male typical
  • sexual behaviour. Its larger size in males is directly organized by prenatal exposure to
  • testosterone (converted to estradiol). Lesions in this area disrupt mounting behaviour
  • in males.

questions.final_answer: in males.

questions.question: Which of the following neurotransmitters is classified as inhibitory? A. Acetylcholine B. Glutamate C. GABA D. Serotonin (, U)
questions.solution_html:
• Hormones play a major role in shaping and regulating sexual behaviour through two
  • main effects – organizational and activational effects. These work together to form the
  • biological basis of sexual motivation and activity.
  • Organizational Effects (Permanent Brain Structuring) - These are long-lasting
  • effects that occur during early development (prenatal or early postnatal period). They
  • help in “organizing” the brain into a male or female pattern. Testosterone is the key
  • hormone. In males, testosterone is converted into estradiol in the brain, which
  • masculinizes and defeminizes the brain.
  • Activational Effects (Temporary Activation in Adulthood) - These are short-term
  • and reversible effects that occur after puberty. Hormones activate the neural circuits
  • formed earlier, controlling sexual desire and behaviour. In females: Estrogen and
  • progesterone levels rise around ovulation, increasing sexual receptivity. In males
  • Testosterone maintains sex drive, erectile function, and sperm production. Removal
  • of testosterone reduces sexual activity, but it can be restored with hormone therapy.
  • Puberty and Hormonal Regulation - During puberty, a surge in sex hormones
  • activates sexual motivation and secondary sexual characteristics. The hypothalamic
  • pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis controls hormone release and reproductive function.
  • Brain Areas and Neurotransmitters - Hormones act on brain regions like the
  • hypothalamus, amygdala, and preoptic area, influencing arousal and partner
  • preference. They interact with dopamine (pleasure), serotonin, and oxytocin (bonding
  • and intimacy).
  • Psychological and Environmental Influence - While hormones set the biological
  • foundation, sexual behaviour is also shaped by learning, emotions, relationships, and
  • cultural factors.
questions.source_exam: BIOPSYCHOLOGY
questions.final_answer: cultural factors.

• Broca's area, located in the left frontal lobe, is critical for the motor aspects of speech
  • production. It is responsible for planning the complex motor sequences required for articulate
  • speech. It sends instructions to the motor cortex to coordinate the muscles of the lips, tongue
  • jaw, and larynx. Result of Damage (Broca's Aphasia): Individuals understand language but
  • have great difficulty producing it. Their speech is non-fluent, effortful, and telegraphic (e.g.
  • "Walk dog today"), but the meaning is often preserved.

questions.question: Explain the process of nerve impulse transmission and the role of neurotransmitters. (, An)
questions.solution_html:
• Hormones play a major role in shaping and regulating sexual behaviour through two
  • main effects – organizational and activational effects. These work together to form the
  • biological basis of sexual motivation and activity.
  • Organizational Effects (Permanent Brain Structuring) - These are long-lasting
  • effects that occur during early development (prenatal or early postnatal period). They
  • help in “organizing” the brain into a male or female pattern. Testosterone is the key
  • hormone. In males, testosterone is converted into estradiol in the brain, which
  • masculinizes and defeminizes the brain.
  • Activational Effects (Temporary Activation in Adulthood) - These are short-term
  • and reversible effects that occur after puberty. Hormones activate the neural circuits
  • formed earlier, controlling sexual desire and behaviour. In females: Estrogen and
  • progesterone levels rise around ovulation, increasing sexual receptivity. In males
  • Testosterone maintains sex drive, erectile function, and sperm production. Removal
  • of testosterone reduces sexual activity, but it can be restored with hormone therapy.
  • Puberty and Hormonal Regulation - During puberty, a surge in sex hormones
  • activates sexual motivation and secondary sexual characteristics. The hypothalamic
  • pituitary–gonadal (HPG) axis controls hormone release and reproductive function.
  • Brain Areas and Neurotransmitters - Hormones act on brain regions like the
  • hypothalamus, amygdala, and preoptic area, influencing arousal and partner
  • preference. They interact with dopamine (pleasure), serotonin, and oxytocin (bonding
  • and intimacy).
  • Psychological and Environmental Influence - While hormones set the biological
  • foundation, sexual behaviour is also shaped by learning, emotions, relationships, and
  • cultural factors.
questions.source_exam: BIOPSYCHOLOGY
questions.final_answer: cultural factors.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the forebrain and explain how each of its major components contributes to higher cognitive and physiological functions.
questions.solution_html:
• The forebrain (or prosencephalon) is the largest and most rostral part of the brain, responsible
  • for the most complex cognitive, sensory, and motor functions. It can be divided into two main
  • parts: the Telencephalon and the Diencephalon.

questions.question: Illustrate the structure of synapse in detail and list out the types of synapses.
questions.solution_html:
• A synapse is a junction with a minute gap that separates two neurons (nerve cells), the
  • basic unit of the nervous system in the brain. Classification Based on Structures - Axo
  • dendritic Synapses, Axo-somatic Synapses, Axo-axonic Synapses, Dendo-dendritic Synapses.
  • Classification Based on Signal Transduction Methods: Electrical Synapses, Chemical
  • Synapses (Excitatory Chemical Synapses, Inhibitory Chemical Synapses). Structure of
  • synapses - The typical synapse comprises three main elements: the presynaptic neuron, the
  • synaptic cleft, and the postsynaptic neuron. Presynaptic Neuron: Synaptic Vesicles, Active
  • Zone, Cytoskeletal Elements. Synaptic Cleft. Postsynaptic Neuron: Functions - Receptor
  • Activation, Ion Flow Regulation
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: Activation, Ion Flow Regulation
